name: Repair equipment on location
summary: When a pump, blender, cementing or coiled tubing unit fails during a job, the field supervisor calls the on-call field mechanic, who first tries to fix it by phone. If a visit is needed the mechanic gathers parts, drives to the pad or rig, completes a hazard assessment and lockout, diagnoses and repairs the unit in the open, tests it with the operator and hands it back, writing a shop repair request when the fix is temporary. Long drives to remote leases, missing parts and winter weather decide how long the crew runs short of equipment.

baseline.org_archetype: A Canadian pressure pumping company with six to eight crewed frac fleets, about 16 cementing units and six coiled tubing crews, maintained from district shops in Alberta and northeast BC.
baseline.notes: Common practice of large WCSB pressure pumpers in 2019-2022: an ERP plant maintenance module for work orders, hour readings from engine controllers and the data van, paper or tablet checklists, spreadsheets and phone calls between shops and field crews.

trigger: A crew on location reports a unit failure and asks for a mechanic.
end_state: The unit is running again on location, fixed by phone, or swapped for another unit and sent to the shop; the call-out work order is closed with hours and parts.

volume.seasonality: Tracks active fleets: highest in the winter season, with spikes in cold snaps when engines, hydraulics and controls fail more often; low in spring break-up and in 2020.

evidence.note: Organisation file volume: about 2-6 call-outs per active frac fleet per week plus cementing and coiled tubing calls. Frac fleets carry backup pumps (src3 notes 20 or more pumps per spread including backups), so many failures are handled by the crew and only some need a field mechanic.

surge.cause: Extreme cold snaps (below about -30 C) raise engine, fuel, hydraulic and control failures on location

evidence.note: Author's estimate from WCSB winter operations; no published count of call-outs opened.
On-call field mechanics answer about 120 call-outs a month; travel to remote leases is most of the time.
Gives remote help on controls and data faults by phone and laptop.
Reports the failure, decides with the mechanic and arranges unit swaps; stands for the cementing and coiled tubing supervisors on their calls. Not listed on this process in the organisation file.
Assigns the on-call mechanic and truck, especially at night. Not listed on this process in the organisation file.

systems.name: Maintenance work order and equipment history module
ERP (finance, procurement, inventory, plant maintenance, billing)
Vehicle telematics and electronic driver logs
Dispatch and crew scheduling board (scheduling module, whiteboards, spreadsheets)
Email, Microsoft Teams and mobile phones
HSE incident, hazard assessment and audit system

resources.name: Crew pickup trucks and light vehicles
Frac pump unit (2,500 to 3,000 HHP, trailer mounted)

steps.name: Report the failure and call for a mechanic
steps.description: The field supervisor or treater sees a pump or unit fail (an engine shutdown, a transmission fault, a hydraulic leak, a control fault), takes it offline, brings on a backup pump if there is one, and phones the on-call mechanic line with the unit number, symptoms and fault codes.

error.defect_description: Symptoms or unit number are passed on incompletely.

evidence.note: Spreads carry backup pumps (src3). Minutes tier C.

steps.name: Troubleshoot by phone
steps.description: The on-call field mechanic talks the operator through checks: reading codes, resetting the controller, checking fuel filters, fluid levels and breakers. Some faults are cleared without a visit.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of heavy equipment maintenance in WCSB pressure pumping companies.

steps.name: Assign a mechanic and truck
steps.description: The dispatcher or shop lead checks which on-call mechanic is free and closest on the dispatch board, opens a call-out work order and gives the mechanic the lease location and access directions.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of heavy equipment maintenance in WCSB pressure pumping companies.

steps.name: Gather parts and tools
steps.description: The mechanic picks likely parts from the base stores or the after-hours parts cage (filters, sensors, hoses, valves), writes them on a sheet for the warehouse to issue later, and loads the service truck.

error.defect_description: Parts taken without an issue transaction, so stock counts and work order costs are wrong.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of heavy equipment maintenance in WCSB pressure pumping companies.

steps.name: Drive to the location
steps.description: The mechanic drives the service truck from the base to the pad or rig, often two to four hours on highway and lease roads; snow, ice and fog slow the drive.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of heavy equipment maintenance in WCSB pressure pumping companies.

steps.name: Check in, orientation and hazard assessment
steps.description: At the lease gate the mechanic signs in with the customer's site supervisor, completes the site orientation if new to the location, and fills in a field level hazard assessment for the repair with the frac crew.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Code Part 2 hazard assessment before work, and customer site orientation rules

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of heavy equipment maintenance in WCSB pressure pumping companies.

steps.name: Lock out the unit and bleed pressure
steps.description: The mechanic and the pump operator isolate the unit from the discharge manifold, bleed trapped pressure from the iron and fluid end, shut the engine down and apply locks under the crew's group lockout.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Code Part 15, sections 212-214: isolate machinery and equipment, verify isolation and apply personal locks before maintenance

evidence.note: Isolation, verification and group lockout (src5). The wait is for a stage to finish so the unit can be isolated (tier C).

steps.name: Diagnose the fault on location
steps.description: The mechanic inspects the unit, reads codes with a laptop and checks pressures, fuel, air and hydraulics to find the failed part, and decides whether it can be fixed on site.

error.defect_description: The wrong cause is found and the fault comes back on test.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of heavy equipment maintenance in WCSB pressure pumping companies.

steps.name: Get remote help on controls
steps.description: The electrical and instrumentation technician joins by phone or video, reviews fault logs the mechanic sends from the laptop and walks through wiring and sensor checks.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of heavy equipment maintenance in WCSB pressure pumping companies.

steps.name: Check parts on hand
steps.description: The mechanic compares the failed part with what is on the service truck and in the fleet's spares trailer, and decides whether to repair now or send for the part from the base.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of heavy equipment maintenance in WCSB pressure pumping companies.

steps.name: Order a parts run
steps.description: The mechanic phones the base warehouse or dispatcher to pull the part and send it out with a hot-shot driver or the next crew truck.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of heavy equipment maintenance in WCSB pressure pumping companies.

steps.name: Wait for the hot-shot delivery
steps.description: A hot-shot carrier or crew truck brings the part from the base, two to six hours on the road, while the mechanic waits on location or helps the crew.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of heavy equipment maintenance in WCSB pressure pumping companies.

steps.name: Repair the unit on location
steps.description: The mechanic replaces the failed part (a sensor, starter, fuel pump, hose, cooler line or valve) in the open on the pad, often in cold and dark, while the crew keeps pumping with the remaining units.

error.defect_description: A temporary fix that fails again within days.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of heavy equipment maintenance in WCSB pressure pumping companies.

steps.name: Test the unit with the operator
steps.description: With locks removed and the area clear, the pump operator starts the unit and runs it against the manifold at low rate while the mechanic watches for leaks and codes.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Code Part 15, section 215.3: returning equipment to operation after locks are removed

evidence.note: Returning to operation after lockout (src5). The wait is for a gap between stages (tier C).

steps.name: Hand the unit back to the crew
steps.description: The mechanic tells the field supervisor the unit is ready, records the repair and downtime on the crew's job log so the lost time can be explained on the field ticket, and notes any follow-up work.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of heavy equipment maintenance in WCSB pressure pumping companies.

steps.name: Decide if shop follow-up is needed
steps.description: The mechanic decides whether the fix is permanent or the unit needs a proper repair in the shop at the next move (a worn component, a leaking seal patched for now).

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of heavy equipment maintenance in WCSB pressure pumping companies.

steps.name: Write the shop repair request
steps.description: The mechanic writes a repair request with the unit number, the temporary fix and the parts likely needed, and sends it to the planner so the shop can book the unit in when it comes home.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of heavy equipment maintenance in WCSB pressure pumping companies.

steps.name: Drive back to the base or next call
steps.description: The mechanic drives back to the base or straight to another call-out; on long trips the mechanic may stop at a camp or hotel when hours of work run out.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of heavy equipment maintenance in WCSB pressure pumping companies.

steps.name: Record the call-out
steps.description: Back at the base, often the next day, the mechanic types the hours, travel, parts sheet and repair notes into the call-out work order and enters the time in the field time system for call-out pay.

error.defect_description: Parts or hours are left off, or the downtime is not linked to the job.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of heavy equipment maintenance in WCSB pressure pumping companies.

steps.name: Review and close the call-out
steps.description: The planner matches the parts sheet with warehouse issues, charges the parts to the unit, checks that any repair request has been booked, and closes the work order.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of heavy equipment maintenance in WCSB pressure pumping companies.

steps.name: Arrange a unit swap
steps.description: When the unit cannot be fixed on site, the field supervisor arranges a replacement unit from the base or another fleet with the dispatcher and the shop, and the failed unit goes home on the next tractor for a shop repair order.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from general knowledge of heavy equipment maintenance in WCSB pressure pumping companies.

exceptions.name: Fixed by phone
exceptions.description: The fault is cleared by the operator with the mechanic's help and no visit is needed.

exceptions.name: Part not on the truck
exceptions.description: The part has to come from the base by hot-shot and the mechanic waits on location.

exceptions.name: Cannot fix on location
exceptions.description: The fault needs the shop; a unit is swapped in and the failed unit goes home for repair.

exceptions.name: Fault persists after repair
exceptions.description: The test shows the fault again and the mechanic goes back to diagnosis.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from the call to the call-out work order closed
benchmarks.population: Field call-outs to frac, cementing and coiled tubing locations at a WCSB pressure pumper, 2019-2022

evidence.note: Author's estimate: the unit is usually back in line 6 to 12 hours after the call, and the work order is typed up and closed within two to four days. No published figure found.

benchmarks.unit: hours from call to unit running

evidence.note: Author's estimate: two to four hours' drive, one to three hours' repair, plus parts runs on a quarter of calls.

pain_points.description: Remote leases mean hours of driving each way, and in winter the drive is slowed by weather, while the fleet runs short a pump.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from WCSB geography (district bases two to four hours from many pads).

pain_points.description: The part needed is often not on the truck, so the mechanic waits for a hot-shot.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

pain_points.description: Repairs in the open in cold and dark are slower and more often temporary, leading to repeat call-outs and shop follow-up.

evidence.note: Maintenance in place is usually less cost-effective and is safer and faster with equipment shut down and lifting equipment available (src3).

pain_points.description: Parts taken from the cage and hours worked are recorded late, so work order costs, stock counts and call-out pay need chasing.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice.

sources.title: Extending Service Life Of Equipment Components Key To Improving Frac Efficiency (Frac Facts, January 2024)
sources.supports: An ideal pump and check valve repair interval is 500 hours, matching a four-well pad so equipment can be maintained between pad moves; a conventional spread uses 20 or more pumps including backups; in-place field maintenance is usually less cost-effective than it appears and maintenance is safer and faster with equipment shut down and lifting equipment available.

sources.title: Occupational Health and Safety Code, Part 15: Managing the Control of Hazardous Energy
sources.supports: Part 15 sections 212 (isolation of machinery, equipment or powered mobile equipment), 213 (verifying isolation), 214 (assigning personal locks), 215 (group control procedures), 215.3 (returning to operation) and 215.4 (isolation of piping). Current page; Part 15 was in force in an earlier edition in 2019-2022.

assumptions: One case is one call from a crew; fleets keep pumping on backup pumps during most call-outs, so the frac-fleet resource is not held, only the failed unit (frac-pump) during diagnosis and repair.
The frac field supervisor role also stands for the cementing and coiled tubing supervisors who make 35 per cent of calls.

The organisation file lists field mechanics and E&I technicians only; dispatchers, field supervisors and the planner also take part, and the mechanic's downtime notes feed non-productive time handling, so a link to fo-frac-screen-out-and-npt-handling is added.
Field mechanics are on call (organisation file shift pattern); night calls wait a little longer for the mechanic to wake and reach the base, covered by the s02 and s03 waits.

Staffing: about 10 FTE stated, close to the hands-on time times 120 calls a month at 130 productive hours. The 20 field mechanics in the organisation file also do shop work and PM on location between calls.
Simulated cycle time runs to the work order being closed; the unit is back in line within hours, the paperwork takes days.
Loaded costs are the organisation file's (wage x 1.35).
